newsitem.title: INDIA: India shuts cheap money window for govt overspending.
newsitem.headline: India shuts cheap money window for govt overspending.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's move to dispense with ad hoc treasury bill auctions shuts a counter for cheap money which the government has used to finance its budget deficits, economists and bankers said on Saturday.
But the step closer to fiscal discipline, by forcing the government to pay more to borrow, will stumble unless spending is controlled, they said.

"The finance minister is banking that a higher cost of borrowing will check fiscal indiscipline," said Aashish Pitale, debt reserach manager at ICICI Securities and Finance Company (I-Sec), Indian affiliate of J.P.Morgan.
Chidambaram said in his 1997/98 (April-March) budget statement on Friday the government will stop its recourse to ad hoc bill issues to finance its deficit from April 1.
Economists say the availability of cheap money through ad hoc bills is one of the major factors for fiscal excesses.
Ad hoc treasury bills are issued at an interest rate of 4.6 percent per annum. The rate of interest on ways and means advances will be mutually agreed upon between RBI and the government.
At present, the government borrows from the market between 7.98 percent per annum (for 91-day treasury bills) to 13.65 percent (for 10-year securities).

Shorn of the treasury bill issue funding option, the government in future will go to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for temporary advances (known as ways and means advances) to tide over temporary mismatches in its receipts and payments.
Ad hoc treasury bills as a means to finance budget deficits have been used since 1954/55.

"It was initiated as an administrative arrangement between the federal government and the RBI so that the government's cash balance should be maintained at a minimum level of 500 million rupees on Fridays and 40 million on other days," the RBI said in a statement.

"To adhere to this arrangement, it became necessary to ensure that the account was replenished by creation of ad hoc treasury bills, whenever the balance fell below the stipulated levels. This resulted in direct monetisation (printing of currency) of budget deficts and contributed to rapid monetary expansion."

"From a monetary and financial system point of view I think the phasing out of the system of ad hoc (treasury bill issues to finance the budget deficit) is an important step," RBI chief Chakravarty Rangarajan said on Friday in a television interview to Star Plus channel.
"I think it will bring about greater fiscal discipline and at the same time give greater autonomy to the RBI," he said.
Economists agreed but warned that the new system could go the same way as the system of ad hoc bills.
"Ad hoc treasury bills also started as a means to tide over temporary shortages," said economist D.R.Pendse. "But it ended up as a means of financing government deficits."
"The new system of ways and means advances will introduce greater fiscal discipline in the government only if the advances are repaid in time," he cautioned.
Other analysts felt the change was only in name.
"Basically the financing will still be done by the RBI," said S. Venkitaramanan former RBI governor. "So the difference is only in name."
Funding by the RBI results in creation of money which adds to inflationary pressures in the economy.
